Post-Selection Distributional Model Evaluation

Amirmohammad Farzaneh Affiliation: Department of Engineering Affiliation: King’s College London Affiliation: London, UK Email: amirmohammad.farzaneh@kcl.ac.uk    Osvaldo Simeone Affiliation: Intelligent Networked Systems Institute (INSI) Affiliation: Northeastern University London Affiliation: London, UK Email: o.simeone@northeastern.edu
Abstract

Formal model evaluation methods typically certify that a model satisfies a prescribed target key performance indicator (KPI) level. However, in many applications, the relevant target KPI level may not be known a priori, and the user may instead wish to compare candidate models by analyzing the full trade-offs between performance and reliability achievable at test time by the models. This task, requiring the reliable estimate of the test-time KPI distributions, is made more complicated by the fact that the same data must often be used both to pre-select a subset of candidate models and to estimate their KPI distributions, causing a potential post-selection bias. In this work, we introduce post-selection distributional model evaluation (PS-DME), a general framework for statistically valid distributional model assessment after arbitrary data-dependent model pre-selection. Building on e-values, PS-DME controls post-selection false coverage rate (FCR) for the distributional KPI estimates and is proved to be more sample efficient than a baseline method based on sample splitting. Experiments on synthetic data, text-to-SQL decoding with large language models, and telecom network performance evaluation demonstrate that PS-DME enables reliable comparison of candidate configurations across a range of reliability levels, supporting the statistically reliable exploration of performance–reliability trade-offs.

1 Introduction

Current formal model selection and evaluation strategies, grounded in multiple hypothesis testing (MHT) (Angelopoulos et al., 2025; Farzaneh and Simeone, 2025), control the probability that the risk measure of interest exceeds a maximum tolerated target value. However, in practice, a suitable target risk level may not be known in advance, and the user may instead wish to explore different trade-offs between test-time performance and reliability. As studied in this paper, this requires estimating the full test-time distribution of the key performance indicator (KPI) of interest for the candidate models.

To exemplify the problem of interest, consider a large language model (LLM) agent that can be deployed on a mobile device with different configurations k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K. As studied in (Huang et al., 2026), these may correspond to models obtained by progressively pruning a base model. Accordingly, the available configurations range from high-quality and high-latency models to lower-quality and lower-latency models. Latency here refers to the prefill delay, which dictates the time to first token. Existing formal model selection methods (Angelopoulos et al., 2025), reviewed in (Farzaneh and Simeone, 2025), require the a priori specification of a latency target. However, as pointed out in (Huang et al., 2026), the latency target may change as the use-cases evolve, and there is a need to understand the full trade-off between performance and reliability.

For example, consider two LLM configurations – a lower-quality, simpler, model and a higher-quality, more complex, model. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), suppose that the user knew the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the latency for the two different configurations. Note that the higher quality model, due to its higher complexity, tends to have a larger latency. If the user tolerates a maximum test-time failure probability γ\gamma, it may prefer the higher-quality model, but only as long as the benefits accrued from higher quality outweigh the larger latency (X2>X1X_{2}>X_{1} in the figure). More generally, the user may also be interested to explore different values of the failure probability γ\gamma in order to obtain more favorable operating points on the trade-off between performance (latency) and test-time reliability 1−γ1-\gamma.

The model selection strategy outlined in the previous example is challenged by the fact that the CDFs of the KPI of interest, e.g., the latency, are not known and must be estimated from data. Furthermore, the configurations being evaluated are often pre-selected from a large pool of candidates to satisfy requirements or criteria such as cost or expected accuracy. Because this pre-selection must generally rely on the same data later used for CDF estimation, naively applying classical confidence bands in this setting yields overly optimistic estimates (see, e.g., (Kuchibhotla, 2025)).

We address these challenges by proposing post-selection distributional model evaluation (PS-DME), a novel formal model evaluation protocol that supports the following steps:

  1. 1)

    Arbitrary model pre-selection: As illustrated in Fig. 1(c), the user can pre-select a subset 𝒦⊆{1,…,K}\mathcal{K}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,K\} of promising configurations using any arbitrary and possibly data-dependent procedure. As shown in Fig. 1(b), we study both data splitting, where one portion of the data is used for pre-selection and the remaining portion is reserved for distributional inference, and in-sample inference, in which the same data serve both for model screening and for uncertainty quantification (Chakraborty et al., 2026).

  2. 2)

    Distributional model evaluation: For each pre-selected configuration k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K}, as illustrated in Fig. 1(d), PS-DME constructs confidence bands for the CDF of the KPI of interest. These bands quantify the uncertainty in the entire distribution of the performance metric, enabling the reliable estimation of quantities such as latency quantiles or outage probabilities (see Fig. 1(a)).

  3. 3)

    Model selection based on performance-reliability trade-off with statistical guarantees: The estimated CDF confidence bands enable the user to compare configurations by examining the trade-off between achievable performance and reliability levels. This allows the user to select a final configuration that strikes the desired balance between performance and reliability, while accounting for statistical uncertainty.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec. 2, we formalize the post-selection distributional model evaluation problem, and introduce the FCR-based validity criterion adopted throughout the paper. Sec. 3 then presents the proposed PS-DME framework together with the sample-splitting baseline, establishes their statistical guarantees, and compares their statistical efficiency through explicit confidence band width comparisons. Sec. 4 positions our contribution with respect to prior work. Sec. 5 validates the proposed methodology on synthetic data, LLM decoding, and telecom performance evaluation. Sec. 6 concludes the paper with a discussion of the main findings and directions for future work, while the appendices collect proofs and extensions.

2 Problem Setup

For a given system, we consider KK candidate configurations indexed by integer k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\}. These may correspond to different hyperparameter settings, decoding strategies, or precision levels. Henceforth, we will refer to each configuration kk as a model. For each model kk, we observe nkn_{k} i.i.d. realizations of a scalar, negatively-oriented, key performance indicator (KPI),

𝒟k={Xk,1,…,Xk,nk},with​Xk,i∼i.i.d.Pk,\mathcal{D}_{k}=\{X_{k,1},\dots,X_{k,n_{k}}\},\quad\text{with}\;X_{k,i}\ \stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\ P_{k}, (1)

where PkP_{k} is an unknown distribution with CDF Fk​(x)=ℙk​(X≤x)F_{k}(x)\ =\ \mathbb{P}_{k}\!\left(X\leq x\right). The datasets 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} can be arbitrarily correlated. For instance, in the case with the same number of data points for all configurations, i.e., nk=nn_{k}=n, the ii-th measures {Xk,i}k=1K\{X_{k,i}\}_{k=1}^{K} may be a function of the same observations, with observations being i.i.d. across index i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n.

Let F^k​(⋅)\widehat{F}_{k}(\cdot) denote the empirical CDF formed from dataset 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} as

F^k(x)=1nk∑i=1nk𝟏{Xk,i≤x}.\widehat{F}_{k}(x)\ =\ \frac{1}{n_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\mathbf{1}\{X_{k,i}\leq x\}. (2)

We study an arbitrary two-step model evaluation pipeline consisting of the following phases:

1) Data-based model pre-selection: Using data 𝒟=∪k=1K𝒟k\mathcal{D}=\cup_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{D}_{k} for all kk configurations, an arbitrary (possibly unknown) data-dependent pre-selection rule produces a subset

𝒦=S⁡(𝒟)⊆{1,…,K}\mathcal{K}\ =\ S\!\left(\mathcal{D}\right)\ \subseteq\ \{1,\dots,K\} (3)

of models.

2) Reliable distributional model evaluation: For each selected model k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K}, we aim to report lower and upper bounds on the CDF Fk​(x)F_{k}(x), i.e.,

Lk​(x)≤Fk​(x)≤Uk​(x),L_{k}(x)\ \leq\ F_{k}(x)\ \leq\ U_{k}(x), (4)

that contain the true CDF uniformly with a user-defined probability.

Formally, for each selected model k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K}, define the miscoverage event

𝒪k={∃x∈ℝ:Fk​(x)∉[Lk​(x),Uk​(x)]},\mathcal{O}_{k}\ =\ \Bigl\{\exists x\in\mathbb{R}:\ F_{k}(x)\notin[L_{k}(x),U_{k}(x)]\Bigr\}, (5)

i.e., the event that there exists a KPI value xx for which the interval [Lk​(x),Uk​(x)][L_{k}(x),U_{k}(x)] does not contain its true CDF value Fk​(x)F_{k}(x) (see Appendix A for an illustration). Post-selection statistical validity is measured via the false coverage proportion (FCP) (Xu et al., 2024). The FCP is defined as the fraction of pre-selected models in set 𝒦\mathcal{K} for which the miscoverage event (5) holds true, i.e.,

FCP=1max⁡{|𝒦|,1}​∑k∈𝒦𝟏​{𝒪k}.\mathrm{FCP}\ =\ \frac{1}{\max\{|\mathcal{K}|,1\}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\mathbf{1}\{\mathcal{O}_{k}\}. (6)

The false coverage rate (FCR) is the expectation of the FCP, i.e.,

FCR=𝔼⁡[FCP],\mathrm{FCR}\ =\ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathrm{FCP}\right], (7)

where 𝟏​{⋅}\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\} is the indicator function, and the expectation is taken with respect to the joint distribution of data 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Note that the selected set 𝒦=S⁡(𝒟)\mathcal{K}=S(\mathcal{D}) is itself data-dependent, and hence its cardinality |𝒦||\mathcal{K}| is a random variable. Our goal is to guarantee the condition

FCR≤δ\mathrm{FCR}\leq\delta (8)

for a user-defined target probability δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1).

3 Post-Selection Distributional Model Evaluation

In order to ensure the condition (8), a conventional approach would adopt a sample splitting strategy, followed by the evaluation of standard uniform confidence intervals for CDFs (Dvoretzky et al., 1956; Massart, 1990). After briefly reviewing this baseline method in Sec. 3.1, we introduce PS-DME in Sec. 3.2. As introduced in Sec. 1, PS-DME leverages the entire dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} for both model selection and distributional model evaluation tasks (see Fig. 1).

3.1 Sample-Splitting Distributional Model Evaluation

For each configuration k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\}, suppose the available data 𝒟k={Xk,1,…,Xk,nk}\mathcal{D}_{k}=\{X_{k,1},\dots,X_{k,n_{k}}\} in (1) are partitioned into two disjoint subsets 𝒟ksel\mathcal{D}_{k}^{\mathrm{sel}} and 𝒟keval\mathcal{D}_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}} of sizes nkseln_{k}^{\mathrm{sel}} and nkevaln_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}} respectively. In the baseline methodology reviewed here, referred to as sample-splitting post-selection distributional model evaluation (SS-DME), the pre-selection subset 𝒟ksel\mathcal{D}_{k}^{\mathrm{sel}} is used exclusively for model selection, while the model evaluation subset 𝒟keval\mathcal{D}_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}} is reserved for distributional inference.

1) Model selection: The selection rule 𝒦=S⁡(𝒟sel)⊆{1,…,K}\mathcal{K}=S\!\left(\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{sel}}\right)\subseteq\{1,\dots,K\} leverages the dataset 𝒟sel=∪k=1K𝒟ksel\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{sel}}=\cup_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{D}_{k}^{\mathrm{sel}} using any arbitrary criterion. For instance, the function S⁡(⋅)S(\cdot) may select the K¯≤K\bar{K}\leq K models with the smallest empirical KPIs X^ksel=∑i=1nkselXk,i/nksel\hat{X}_{k}^{\text{sel}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}^{\text{sel}}}X_{k,i}/n_{k}^{\text{sel}}.

2) Distributional inference: For each selected configuration k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K}, SS-DME constructs a uniform confidence band for the true CDF Fk​(⋅)F_{k}(\cdot) using only the inference subset 𝒟keval\mathcal{D}_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}}. This is elaborated on in the rest of this subsection.

Let F^keval​(⋅)\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}}(\cdot) denote the empirical CDF constructed from data 𝒟keval\mathcal{D}_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}} using (2). By the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz (DKW) inequality (Dvoretzky et al., 1956), for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 we have

ℙ⁡(supx∈ℝ|F^keval​(x)−Fk​(x)|>ε)≤2​exp⁡(−2​nkeval​ε2).\mathbb{P}\!\left(\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\big|\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}}(x)-F_{k}(x)\big|>\varepsilon\right)\leq 2\exp\!\left(-2n_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}}\varepsilon^{2}\right). (9)

Using this inequality, SS-DME constructs the confidence bounds as

Lk​(x)\displaystyle L_{k}(x) =max⁡{0,F^keval​(x)−εk},\displaystyle=\max\!\{0,\,\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}}(x)-\varepsilon_{k}\}, (10a)
andUk​(x)\displaystyle\text{and}\quad U_{k}(x) =min⁡{1,F^keval​(x)+εk},\displaystyle=\min\!\{1,\,\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}}(x)+\varepsilon_{k}\}, (10b)

where

εk=12​nkeval​log⁡(2​Kδ​|𝒦|).\varepsilon_{k}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2n_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}}}\log\!\left(\frac{2K}{\delta|\mathcal{K}|}\right)}. (11)

SS-DME provides the following guarantee.

Lemma 1.

For any pre-selection rule S⁡(⋅)S(\cdot), the confidence bands 𝒞k=[Lk​(x),Uk​(x)]\mathcal{C}_{k}=[L_{k}(x),U_{k}(x)] produced by SS-DME, where Lk​(x)L_{k}(x) and Uk​(x)U_{k}(x) are defined by (10a) and (10b), respectively, satisfy the requirement FCR≤δ\mathrm{FCR}\leq\delta.

A proof of Lemma 1 can be found in Appendix C.

3.2 In-Sample Distributional Model Evaluation

The SS-DME strategy described in Sec. 3.1 ensures validity by enforcing independence between model selection and distributional inference. However, this separation reduces the effective sample size available for constructing confidence bands, potentially leading to occasionally wide intervals. In this subsection, we introduce PS-DME, which enables full-data reuse while maintaining the requirement (8) on the FCR. To achieve this, PS-DME adopts the framework of e-values (Ramdas and Wang, 2025) to construct confidence intervals with post-selection validity (Xu et al., 2024).

E-values are statistics used to test null hypotheses that have additional properties of robustness as compared to p-values, including, notably, the support of the post-hoc selection of the significance level (Vovk and Wang, 2021; Koning, 2025). An e-value can be constructed from a p-value via the application of an e-calibrator function, which is defined as follows.

Definition 1 (e-calibrator).

A function f:[0,1]→[0,∞]f:[0,1]\to[0,\infty] is called an e-calibrator if it satisfies the following properties: (i) ff is nonincreasing and upper semicontinuous; and (ii) ∫01f⁡(u)​𝑑u≤1\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}f(u)\,du\leq 1.

For example, a commonly used family of e-calibrators is given by the functions

fτ​(p)=(1−τ)​p−τ,τ∈(0,1).f_{\tau}(p)=(1-\tau)\,p^{-\tau},\qquad\tau\in(0,1). (12)

An optimal e-calibrator would yield the largest e-value across all possible p-values p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1]. However, within the family (12), no single value of parameter τ\tau yields the largest e-value fτ​(p)f_{\tau}(p) for all possible values of p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] (Vovk and Wang, 2021). Therefore, the optimal choice of τ\tau is non-trivial, and a common selection is τ=1/2\tau=1/2 (Yanchenko et al., 2025).

For any e-calibrator f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot), define its generalized inverse as f−1​(t)=sup{u∈[0,1]:f⁡(u)≥t}f^{-1}(t)=\sup\{u\in[0,1]:f(u)\geq t\}.

For each configuration k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\}, let F^k​(⋅)\widehat{F}_{k}(\cdot) denote the empirical CDF formed by (2) using the entire dataset 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}. For an arbitrary e-calibrator f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot), PS-DME produces the bounds

Lk​(x)\displaystyle L_{k}(x) =max⁡{0,F^k​(x)−εk},\displaystyle=\max\!\{0,\,\widehat{F}_{k}(x)-\varepsilon_{k}\}, (13a)
andUk​(x)\displaystyle\text{and}\quad U_{k}(x) =min⁡{1,F^k​(x)+εk},\displaystyle=\min\!\{1,\,\widehat{F}_{k}(x)+\varepsilon_{k}\}, (13b)

with band width

εk=12​nk​log⁡(2f−1​(Kδ​|𝒦|)).\varepsilon_{k}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2n_{k}}\log\!\left(\frac{2}{f^{-1}\!\left(\frac{K}{\delta|\mathcal{K}|}\right)}\right)}. (14)

Using the properties of e-values (Vovk and Wang, 2021), PS-DME can be shown to have the following validity property, which is proved in Appendix D.

Theorem 1.

For any selection rule S⁡(⋅)S(\cdot) and for any e-calibrator f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot), the confidence bands in (13a) and (13b) produced by PS-DME satisfy the requirement (8), i.e., FCR≤δ\mathrm{FCR}\leq\delta.

An alternative implementation of PS-DME that leverages Berk-Jones (BJ) confidence bounds (Berk and Jones, 1979) instead of the DKW inequality (9) is presented in Appendix F. BJ confidence bounds are implicitly defined based on likelihood ratios, yielding input-dependent confidence band widths. This contrasts with the sup-norm form of the DKW statistic (9), which yields efficient, symmetric, and input-independent confidence widths (14).

3.3 Comparing SS-DME and PS-DME

Thanks to its use of the full dataset for distributional inference, PS-DME can be more efficient than SS-DME. In fact, a direct comparison of the band widths (14) and (11) yields an explicit condition under which PS-DME yields a narrower band than SS-DME as follows.

Lemma 2.

For a pre-selection set size |𝒦||\mathcal{K}|, the band width of PS-DME (14) is smaller than that of SS-DME (11) if and only if the inequality

nkevalnk<log⁡(2​Kδ​|𝒦|)log⁡(2f−1​(Kδ​|𝒦|))\frac{n_{k}^{\text{eval}}}{n_{k}}<\frac{\log\!\left(\frac{2K}{\delta|\mathcal{K}|}\right)}{\log\!\left(\frac{2}{f^{-1}\!\left(\frac{K}{\delta|\mathcal{K}|}\right)}\right)} (15)

holds.

The condition (15) highlights the fundamental trade-off between the two methods. PS-DME benefits from using the full sample size nkn_{k} for both pre-selection and inference, but it pays an additional post-selection correction factor captured by the term f−1​(K/δ​|𝒦|)f^{-1}\!\left(K/{\delta|\mathcal{K}|}\right). In contrast, SS-DME avoids this correction by enforcing separation between pre-selection and inference, but it uses only the reduced sample size nkevaln_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}}.

Using the e-calibrator family (12), the result in Lemma 2 can be specialized as follows (see Appendix E for a proof).

Corollary 2.

Assume that the e-calibrator belongs to the power family (12). A necessary condition for the PS-DME width (14) to be smaller than the SS-DME width (11) is

nkevalnk<log⁡(2​Kδ​|𝒦|)log⁡2−W⁡(−δ​|𝒦|e​K),\frac{n_{k}^{\text{eval}}}{n_{k}}<\frac{\log\!\left(\frac{2K}{\delta|\mathcal{K}|}\right)}{\log 2-W\!\left(-\frac{\delta|\mathcal{K}|}{eK}\right)}, (16)

where W⁡(⋅)W(\cdot) denotes the lower real branch of the Lambert WW function, i.e., the inverse of the function f⁡(w)=w​ewf(w)=we^{w} on the interval [−1/e,0)[-1/e,0). Furthermore, when the candidate set size |𝒦||\mathcal{K}| is fixed and does not depend on the data 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}, if condition (16) holds, there exists a value of the constant τ\tau for which the width (14) of PS-DME is smaller than the width of SS-DME (11), namely

τ=−1W⁡(−δ​|𝒦|e​K).\tau=-\frac{1}{W\!\left(-\frac{\delta|\mathcal{K}|}{eK}\right)}. (17)

An illustration of this result can be found in Appendix A.

4 Related Work

Referring to Appendix B for further details, we highlight here connections to the literature on post-selection inference.

In the literature on inference after data-dependent selection (Lee et al., 2016; Taylor and Tibshirani, 2018), the FCR criterion was introduced in (Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2005) as an analog of the false discovery rate for confidence intervals. More recently, reference (Xu et al., 2024) developed general procedures for controlling FCR under arbitrary data-dependent selection. This methodology leverages e-values for their in-sample post-selection validity (Grünwald, 2024; Vovk and Wang, 2021). Related work has clarified the connection between e-values, post-hoc p-values, and data-dependent testing procedures (Koning, 2023; Chugg et al., 2026).

In concurrent work, leveraging the framework of e-values, reference (Koobs and Koning, 2026) developed a mechanism for obtaining confidence intervals based on data-dependent confidence levels. Framing the contribution in the context of the present work, the method in (Koobs and Koning, 2026) applies to a single model and to a fixed statistic, e.g., the average risk. Therefore, it cannot be leveraged for model selection, as well as for exploring the test-time trade-offs between performance and reliability.

5 Experiments

5.1 Benchmarks and Performance Measures

In this section, we compare three distributional model evaluation strategies by leveraging different metrics capturing reliability and efficiency for both performance evaluation and final selection.

5.1.1 Distributional Model Evaluation Strategies

We compare the following strategies:

1) Sample-splitting distributional model evaluation (SS-DME): As described in Sec. 3.1, SS-DME partitions the dataset for each configuration into independent selection and inference subsets. Model selection is carried out using the selection split, and CDF bands are constructed on the inference split via the DKW-based confidence intervals (10a) and (10b).

2) Naive in-sample distributional model evaluation (N-PS-DME): This benchmark reuses the full dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} for both model selection and distributional inference, applying the same construction (10a)-(10b) as in SS-DME with nkn_{k} in place of nkevaln_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}}. Due to selection bias, N-PS-DME cannot generally guarantee the FCR requirement (8).

3) In-sample distributional model evaluation (PS-DME): The proposed PS-DME, detailed in Sec. 3.2, reuses the full dataset for both selection and inference, leveraging an e-value-based methodology to construct valid post-hoc CDF bounds (13a) and (13b) that satisfy the FCR condition (8). Unless otherwise stated, we use the power e-calibrator (12) with the optimal parameter τ\tau calculated as discussed in Sec. 3.3.

5.1.2 Performance Measures

We adopt the following metrics to assess both reliability and efficiency of different strategies.

1) False coverage proportion (FCP): For each simulated trial, we compute the realized FCP as defined in (6), namely the fraction of selected configurations k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K} for which the miscoverage event 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k} in (5) occurs. Averaging across repetitions yields an empirical estimate of the FCR (7).

2) Confidence band width: We quantify statistical efficiency via the average uniform band radius. For SS-DME and N-PS-DME this corresponds to εk\varepsilon_{k} in (11), and for PS-DME to εk\varepsilon_{k} in (14). We report averages across selected configurations and experimental repetitions.

3) Post-selection guaranteed KPI: With reference to the example in Fig. 1(a), suppose that the system under study has a maximum allocated failure probability equal to γ\gamma. Using the lower bound Lk​(x)L_{k}(x), each configuration kk can guarantee a KPI no worse than

Xk∗=inf{x:Lk​(x)≥1−γ},X_{k}^{*}=\inf\{x:L_{k}(x)\geq 1-\gamma\}, (18)

while satisfying an error rate (FCR) no larger than δ\delta. We provide an illustration of this definition in Fig. 3, which is further discussed in the next section. Upon optimization over the configuration k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K}, the post-selection best guaranteed KPI is thus given by X∗=mink∈𝒦⁡Xk∗X^{*}=\min_{k\in\mathcal{K}}X^{*}_{k}.

5.2 Synthetic Data

We begin by validating the proposed PS-DME in a fully controlled synthetic setting, where the true data-generating distribution is known exactly. This allows us to directly assess both coverage properties and the tightness of the resulting CDF bands.

Setup: We consider a standard linear-Gaussian model with covariates drawn as U∼𝒩⁡(0,I10)U\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{10}), and responses generated according to the linear model V=U⊤​β+εV=U^{\top}\beta+\varepsilon, with noise ε∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) and coefficient vector β∼𝒩⁡(0,I10)\beta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{10}) whose entries are held fixed for all data points.

We construct K=2000K=2000 candidate predictors g^k​(⋅)\widehat{g}_{k}(\cdot) by training ridge regression models over a logarithmically spaced grid of regularization parameters λ1,…,λK\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{K}, where the grid spans the interval [10−4,102][10^{-4},10^{2}]. Each model is trained on an independent training dataset of size 600. For each model kk, the KPI is defined as the squared prediction error Xk,i=(Vi−g^k​(Ui))2X_{k,i}=(V_{i}-\widehat{g}_{k}(U_{i}))^{2}, evaluated on the same independent calibration dataset {(Ui,Vi)}i=1n\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} of size nn. Thus, for each model kk, we have the KPI samples 𝒟k={Xk,i}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{k}=\{X_{k,i}\}_{i=1}^{n} that are i.i.d. draws from an unknown distribution PkP_{k}, and samples {Xk,i}k=1K\{X_{k,i}\}_{k=1}^{K} are correlated across different hyperparameters. Model pre-selection chooses the M=1000M=1000 configurations with the smallest empirical mean KPI. Throughout all experiments, we target an FCR level δ=0.1\delta=0.1 in the requirement (8).

Results: To start, we illustrate the per-configuration CDF estimates produced by different schemes for a given candidate hyperparameter, selected here as λk=0.0231\lambda_{k}=0.0231. Fig. 2 plots the corresponding true risk CDF Fk​(x)F_{k}(x), the empirical CDF F^k​(x)\widehat{F}_{k}(x), and the corresponding post-selection confidence band [Lk​(x),Uk​(x)][L_{k}(x),U_{k}(x)] provided by SS-DME, N-PS-DME, and PS-DME using a calibration dataset of size n=20n=20. For SS-DME, we use 50% of the available calibration dataset for pre-selection, and the remainder 50% for inference. In this example, while SS-DME and PS-DME provide miscoverage control, N-PS-DME exhibits a miscoverage event. This illustrates the general theoretical result that SS-DME and PS-DME offer the FCR requirement (8), while N-PS-DME does not provide error control guarantees due to selection bias.

Fig. 2 also confirms the comparison between the widths of SS-DME and PS-DME formalized by Lemma 2. For the given split, the condition (15) is satisfied, and accordingly, the band width achieved by PS-DME is markedly narrower than that of SS-DME. As detailed in Sec. 3.2, this can be attributed to the fact that PS-DME uses the entire calibration dataset for forming the bands, while SS-DME is forced to use only a subset of the dataset for inference. As highlighted in the figure, this improved efficiency allows PS-DME to select a KPI Xk∗X^{*}_{k} in (18) that is smaller, and thus preferable, than SS-DME.

We now turn to further analyzing the post-selection guaranteed KPI. Fig. 3 reports the best post-selection guaranteed KPI as a function of the target probability γ\gamma for SS-DME and for PS-DME. N-PS-DME does not guarantee FCR control, and thus is not included in this analysis. PS-DME is seen to achieve uniformly lower KPI (quadratic error) across all values of target probability 1−γ1-\gamma. Highest benefits are observed in the regimes of low test-time failure rates γ\gamma and when calibration data are scarce, i.e., for n=20n=20. In fact, in a low-sample regime, SS-DME suffers from a severe reduction in effective inference sample size, since only a fraction of the already limited data is available for band construction.

5.3 Evaluating and Selecting LLM Decoding Configurations

We next instantiate the proposed PS-DME in a text-to-SQL task performed by an LLM, where the KPI is a score accounting for the quality of the generated SQL query.

Task and dataset: We consider the text-to-SQL Spider benchmark (Yu et al., 2018), in which the LLM receives as input (i) a natural-language question, (ii) a database identifier specifying which database the question refers to, and (iii) the corresponding database schema, including table names, columns, and their relationships. The goal of the model is to generate an SQL query that, when executed on the specified database, correctly answers the natural-language question. Performance is evaluated by comparing the execution result of the generated query with that of the gold (ground-truth) SQL query provided in the dataset. In our experiments, we restrict attention to a fixed subset of n=200n=200 (randomly selected) validation examples from Spider (Yu et al., 2018).

We adopt the Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct LLM (Yang et al., 2024) with nucleus (top-pp) sampling (Holtzman et al., 2019), with parameters given by top_p∈{0.90,0.95}\texttt{top\_p}\in\{0.90,0.95\} and temperature τ∈{0.3,0.7,1.0}\tau\in\{0.3,0.7,1.0\}. The maximum output length is 160160 tokens.

The hyperparameters correspond to decoding strategies that trade off computational budget against solution quality. In total, we consider K=43K=43 candidate configurations, organized into three families:

(i) Single decode: We include one greedy (deterministic) decoding together with the six stochastic single-pass decoding strategies obtained by varying top_p∈{0.90,0.95}\texttt{top\_p}\in\{0.90,0.95\} and temperature τ∈{0.3,0.7,1.0}\tau\in\{0.3,0.7,1.0\}.

(ii) Best-of-nn (BoN) decoding: Best-of-nn sampling (Brown et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022) generates n∈{2,4,6}n\in\{2,4,6\} independent SQL candidates for the same input, and selects the one achieving the highest reward. For each value of parameter nn, we vary temperature τ∈{0.3,0.7,1.0}\tau\in\{0.3,0.7,1.0\} and top_p∈{0.90,0.95}\texttt{top\_p}\in\{0.90,0.95\}, yielding 18 BoN configurations.

(iii) Iterative draft–refine (IAD) decoding: Iterative self-refinement methods (Madaan et al., 2023) improve outputs by repeatedly conditioning on previous drafts. Starting from an initial draft SQL generated from the prompt, the model produces revised SQL queries conditioned on the previous draft. This process is repeated for up to t∈{2,4,6}t\in\{2,4,6\} iterations, after which the final SQL query is returned. For each value of tt, we vary temperature τ∈{0.3,0.7,1.0}\tau\in\{0.3,0.7,1.0\} and top_p∈{0.90,0.95}\texttt{top\_p}\in\{0.90,0.95\}, yielding 18 IAD configurations.

To evaluate the quality of a generated SQL query, we construct a performance metric that captures both structural similarity at the token level and semantic correctness relative to the reference query. The token-level KPI measures the overlap between the SQL tokens appearing in the predicted and reference queries using the F1 score, i.e., the harmonic mean of precision and recall. The semantic correctness measure determines whether the generated query retrieves the correct information from the database leveraging the F1 score (Yu et al., 2018). The final KPI is given by 1−w​F​1token−(1−w)​F​1exec1-wF1_{\text{token}}-(1-w)F1_{\text{exec}}, where F​1tokenF1_{\text{token}} and F​1execF1_{\text{exec}} are the discussed F1 scores. We set w=0.3w=0.3, assigning greater importance to execution-level correctness, since the primary objective of a text-to-SQL system is to retrieve the correct database result.

Results: Fig. 4 compares the post-selection guaranteed KPI achieved by SS-DME, which uses a fraction nsel/n∈{0.1,0.2,0.3}n^{\text{sel}}/n\in\{0.1,0.2,0.3\} of the dataset for pre-selection, with that obtained by the proposed PS-DME. As shown in the figure, PS-DME consistently guarantees lower KPI values, corresponding to higher performance for the selected decoding strategy.

6 Conclusion

We introduced PS-DME, a framework for statistically valid distributional evaluation of pre-selected models under full data reuse. By leveraging e-values, the proposed method constructs post-selection confidence bands for entire CDFs with guaranteed false coverage rate control, addressing the bias induced by data-dependent model selection.

Unlike conventional target-based approaches, PS-DME enables uncertainty-aware assessment of the full KPI distribution, supporting reliable exploration of performance–reliability trade-offs across operating points such as latency quantiles and outage levels. Compared to sample splitting, PS-DME can yield narrower confidence bands when the efficiency gains from full data reuse outweigh the cost of post-selection correction, as formalized through explicit width comparisons.

Experiments on synthetic data, LLM decoding, and telecom evaluation demonstrate that PS-DME achieves valid post-selection inference while often providing tighter bands and stronger guarantees than sample-splitting baselines.

Future work includes extending the framework to more general and multivariate performance measures, developing sharper confidence band constructions, and integrating distributional guarantees into downstream decision-making for reliable model deployment.

Appendix B Additional Related Work

Reliable hyperparameter selection:

Recent work has shown that hyperparameter selection can be cast as an MHT problem, enabling finite-sample guarantees for the selected model (Angelopoulos et al., 2025). This framework has been extended to a variety of performance criteria and engineering applications (Stephen et al., 2021; Bates et al., 2023; Angelopoulos et al., 2022); see (Farzaneh and Simeone, 2025) for a recent review. A key limitation of this literature is that it focuses on scalar performance metrics, e.g., average risk, relative to a pre-specified target level. In contrast, this work aims at distributional evaluation, enabling comparison of models across all test-time reliability levels without committing to a single KPI threshold.

Confidence bands for distribution functions:

Classical nonparametric methods provide confidence bands for a single distribution function, notably via the DKW inequality (Dvoretzky et al., 1956; Massart, 1990). Likelihood-ratio and goodness-of-fit approaches, such as Berk–Jones and empirical likelihood methods (see Appendix F), can yield tighter or more adaptive bands (Berk and Jones, 1979; Owen, 1995; Dümbgen and Wellner, 2023). However, these methods are designed for marginal inference and do not account for model selection. In contrast, our setting requires validity after arbitrary data-dependent screening.

Appendix E Proof of Corollary 2

The Vovk–Sellke bound (Vovk and Wang, 2021) states that for the power family of calibrators (12) we have

fVS​(p)=maxτ∈(0,1)⁡fτ​(p)={−exp⁡(−1)p​log⁡p,p≤e−1,1,p>e−1,f_{\mathrm{VS}}(p)=\max_{\tau\in(0,1)}f_{\tau}(p)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{-\exp(-1)}{p\log p},&p\leq e^{-1},\\[6.0pt] 1,&p>e^{-1},\end{cases} (33)

where

arg⁡maxτ∈(0,1)​fτ​(p)=−1log⁡p\arg\max_{\tau\in(0,1)}f_{\tau}(p)=-\frac{1}{\log p} (34)

Hence, for all p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) and τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1), the inequality

fτ​(p)≤fVS​(p)f_{\tau}(p)\leq f_{\mathrm{VS}}(p) (35)

holds. Note, however, that the function fVS​(p)f_{\mathrm{VS}}(p) is not a valid e-calibrator.

Since function fτ​(⋅)f_{\tau}(\cdot) is decreasing, the corresponding inverse satisfies the inequality fτ−1​(y)≤fVS−1​(y)f_{\tau}^{-1}(y)\leq f_{\mathrm{VS}}^{-1}(y) for all y≥1y\geq 1. Furthermore, the inverse of the Vovk-Sellke bound is given by

fVS−1​(y)=exp⁡(W−1​(−1e​y))f_{\mathrm{VS}}^{-1}(y)=\exp\!\left(W_{-1}\!\left(-\frac{1}{ey}\right)\right) (36)

for p≤e−1p\leq e^{-1}. Substituting y=K/(δ​|𝒦|)y=K/(\delta|\mathcal{K}|) in (36) and plugging the result in the inequality (15) yields the condition (16). Given (35), the inequality (15) for any τ\tau implies (16), proving the necessity of condition (16). Furthermore, using (34), we obtain that the maximizing choice of the power-calibrator parameter at level y=K/(δ​|𝒦|)y=K/(\delta|\mathcal{K}|) is (17). Therefore, when |𝒦||\mathcal{K}| is fixed, condition (16) ensures that this choice of τ\tau makes (15) hold, completing the proof.

Appendix F Alternative Implementation of PS-DME via Berk–Jones CDF Bands

The proof of Theorem 1 in Appendix D shows that PS-DME applies to any valid test of the null hypothesis ℋ0,k​(F)\mathcal{H}_{0,k}(F) in (21). While Sec. 3 uses the Kolmogorov statistic Tk​(F)T_{k}(F) in (22) together with the DKW inequality (9), one may instead use likelihood-ratio-type goodness-of-fit statistics such as the Berk–Jones (BJ) statistic (Berk and Jones, 1979).

Define the BJ statistic for a candidate CDF FF as

Snk​(F)=supx∈ℝK⁡(F^k​(x),F⁡(x)),S_{n_{k}}(F)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}K\!\bigl(\widehat{F}_{k}(x),\,F(x)\bigr), (37)

where K⁡(⋅,⋅)K(\cdot,\cdot) is the Bernoulli KL divergence defined as

K⁡(a,b)=a​log⁡(ab)+(1−a)​log⁡(1−a1−b),a,b∈(0,1).K(a,b)=a\log\!\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)+(1-a)\log\!\left(\frac{1-a}{1-b}\right),\qquad a,b\in(0,1). (38)

Under the null hypothesis ℋ0,k​(F)\mathcal{H}_{0,k}(F) and assuming that FF is continuous, the probability integral transform implies that the transformed variables Uk,i=F⁡(Xk,i)U_{k,i}=F(X_{k,i}) are i.i.d. Unif⁡[0,1]\mathrm{Unif}[0,1] (Shorack and Wellner, 2009). Let G^\widehat{G} denote the empirical CDF of {Uk,i}i=1nk\{U_{k,i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{k}}. Then, under the null, the statistic Snk​(F)S_{n_{k}}(F) in (37) has the same distribution as

Snk(0)=supu∈[0,1]K⁡(G^​(u),u),S_{n_{k}}^{(0)}=\sup_{u\in[0,1]}K\!\bigl(\widehat{G}(u),\,u\bigr), (39)

i.e., the BJ statistic computed from an i.i.d. sample drawn from Unif⁡[0,1]\mathrm{Unif}[0,1].

Let qnk​(1−α)q_{n_{k}}(1-\alpha) denote the (1−α)(1-\alpha) quantile of the null distribution of random variable Snk(0)S_{n_{k}}^{(0)} in (39). Then, by test inversion (Owen, 1995; Jager and Wellner, 2007), the acceptance region

Snk​(F)≤qnk​(1−α)S_{n_{k}}(F)\leq q_{n_{k}}(1-\alpha) (40)

defines a valid (1−α)(1-\alpha) confidence set for the true CDF FkF_{k}. This condition is equivalent to requiring that, for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, the value F⁡(x)F(x) lies in the set of all u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1] satisfying

K⁡(F^k​(x),u)≤qnk​(1−α).K\!\bigl(\widehat{F}_{k}(x),\,u\bigr)\leq q_{n_{k}}(1-\alpha). (41)

Accordingly, the lower and upper bounds at each xx are obtained by solving this inequality for uu, yielding confidence bands

Lk​(x)≤Fk​(x)≤Uk​(x),∀x∈ℝ,L_{k}(x)\leq F_{k}(x)\leq U_{k}(x),\qquad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}, (42)

which depend on the local value F^k​(x)\widehat{F}_{k}(x) and are generally asymmetric.

Compared to the DKW-based bands in (13a)–(13b), whose width is the input-independent quantity εk\varepsilon_{k} in (14), the BJ bands are input-dependent. In particular, they are typically tighter in the tails and wider around the center of the CDF, reflecting the geometry of the KL divergence: deviations are penalized more strongly when F^k​(x)\widehat{F}_{k}(x) is close to 00 or 11, and more weakly near F^k​(x)≈1/2\widehat{F}_{k}(x)\approx 1/2 (Jager and Wellner, 2007). This improved adaptivity comes at the cost of computing the critical value qnk​(1−α)q_{n_{k}}(1-\alpha), e.g., via Noé’s recursion (Noé, 1972), and solving a one-dimensional root-finding problem for each value of F^k​(x)\widehat{F}_{k}(x).

We finally compare the default DKW-based implementation of PS-DME in (13a)–(13b) with the BJ-based implementation described above. Fig. 7(a) shows the confidence bands obtained by the two methods for a representative hyperparameter. The BJ-based band is tighter in the tails of the CDF and wider around the center, in agreement with the discussion above.

The impact of this difference on model evaluation is illustrated in Fig. 7(b), which reports the post-selection best guaranteed KPI as a function of the target outage probability γ\gamma. The BJ-based implementation provides a stronger guarantee for most outage levels, particularly in the tail regimes. In contrast, for intermediate outage probabilities, the DKW-based implementation can yield slightly tighter guarantees, reflecting its uniform band width in (14).

Appendix G Additional Experiments

G.1 Evaluating and Selecting Telecom Network Configurations

We evaluate the proposed PS-DME on a wireless networking dataset derived from an Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) deployment (Bonati et al., 2021).

G.1.1 Dataset and system setup

We use the dataset introduced in (Bonati et al., 2021), which was collected on the Colosseum wireless network emulator at Northeastern University (Polese et al., 2023). The dataset contains measurements from an O-RAN deployment consisting of four base stations operating with a channel bandwidth of 33 MHz, consisting of 1515 physical resource blocks (PRBs), and serving 4040 user equipments (UEs). Traffic is organized into three slices representing distinct service classes, namely enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB), massive machine-type communications (MTC), and ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC) (Popovski et al., 2018). The dataset reports periodic slice-level measurements, including the downlink buffer occupancy and downlink transmission rate for each slice, across different network configurations, which specify (i) the scheduling policy used for each slice; and (ii) the initial allocation of radio resources, i.e., PRBs, across slices. Specifically, the dataset specifies 1818 predefined configurations, each corresponding to one particular combination of one of three schedulers and of one of six initial allocations for the three slices. We adopt the downlink buffer occupancy for the URLLC slice as the (negatively oriented) KPI Xk,iX_{k,i}. The ground truth CDF of this KPI is estimated for each configuration by using 90%90\% of the available data.

Model pre-selection is performed by selecting the six configurations with the smallest empirical mean buffer occupancy for the URLLC slice.

G.1.2 Results

Fig. 8 illustrates representative post-selection CDF bands for a selected O-RAN configuration for SS-DME and PS-DME, with SS-DME using half of the calibration data for pre-selection. The horizontal axis corresponds to the buffer occupancy KPI, while the vertical axis shows the corresponding CDF. As in the previous experiments, SS-DME yields wider bands compared to PS-DME. Additionally, because SS-DME uses fewer calibration samples to estimate the empirical CDF, its empirical CDF exhibits larger deviations from the proxy true CDF than that of PS-DME. Note also that, since SS-DME uses a subset of the calibration dataset for evaluating the empirical CDF, the empirical CDFs for SS-DME and PS-DME are different.

We then analyze the post-selection guaranteed KPI. Fig. 9 reports the best guaranteed buffer occupancy as a function of the target probability 1−γ1-\gamma for PS-DME, as well as SS-DME with dataset split ratios nsel/nn^{\text{sel}}/n from the set {0.2,0.3,0.4}\{0.2,0.3,0.4\}. The proposed PS-DME consistently yields stronger guarantees than the SS-DME variants.

To further investigate the trade-off induced by sample splitting, we fix two target probabilities, 1−γ∈{0.7,0.8}1-\gamma\in\{0.7,0.8\}, and vary the split ratio nsel/nn^{\mathrm{sel}}/n used by SS-DME. Fig. 10 reports the resulting best guaranteed buffer occupancy as a function of the split ratio. The two panels correspond to different calibration regimes: Fig. 10(a) uses 30%30\% of the available data for calibration, while Fig. 10(b) uses the entire available dataset. In each panel, we report results for both target probabilities 1−γ=0.71-\gamma=0.7 and 1−γ=0.81-\gamma=0.8.

In the low-calibration regime shown in Fig. 10(a), SS-DME consistently yields a larger best guaranteed buffer occupancy than PS-DME across all split ratios and both target probabilities. This reflects the fact that splitting an already limited calibration dataset reduces the effective sample size available for both model selection and inference, leading to more conservative guarantees and hence worse (larger) guaranteed KPI values. In contrast, in the high-calibration regime shown in Fig. 10(b), the trade-off becomes more nuanced. For intermediate values of the split ratio, SS-DME can outperform PS-DME for the less stringent target 1−γ=0.71-\gamma=0.7, achieving a smaller guaranteed buffer occupancy. This improvement arises because allocating a moderate portion of the data to selection can lead to better configuration choices, while the remaining data are still sufficient to yield tight confidence bands. However, this advantage does not persist uniformly across all split ratios or for the more stringent target 1−γ=0.81-\gamma=0.8, where the need for precise distributional estimation favors PS-DME, which leverages the full dataset.

G.2 Post-Selection CDF Inference for Server Latency

We next evaluate the proposed PS-DME confidence bands on response-time distributions extracted from HTTP server access logs. Latency is a canonical KPI in web services and distributed systems, where configurations are routinely compared and selected based on empirical performance measured on the same data (Dean and Barroso, 2013; Barroso et al., 2019). This setting provides a natural testbed for post-selection CDF inference, as distributional information, rather than a single scalar metric, is often of primary interest.

G.2.1 Setup

We consider a collection of HTTP server access logs obtained from a publicly available server log dataset released on Kaggle and commonly used for benchmarking log analysis and anomaly detection methods (Kaggle Contributors, 2020). Each log entry records, among other fields, the HTTP request method, the request path, and the response time measured at the server. In this experiment, the hyperparameters correspond to discrete request-handling configurations defined by ordered pairs (HTTP method,request path)(\text{HTTP method},\text{request path}). The HTTP method takes values in {GET,POST,PUT,DELETE}\{\texttt{GET},\texttt{POST},\texttt{PUT},\texttt{DELETE}\}, which comprise all methods observed in the dataset. The request path is defined as the URL path component of the request line, with query parameters removed, and takes values in the finite set of distinct paths observed across the log file.

To construct a finite hyperparameter grid, we enumerate all method–path pairs appearing in the dataset and compute their total frequency. We retain only those pairs that appear at least Nmin=200N_{\min}=200 times, ensuring that each candidate configuration admits sufficiently many samples for stable empirical CDF estimation. Among the remaining pairs, we select the K=30K=30 most frequent configurations to form a fixed hyperparameter grid, which is determined once and held constant across all experimental repetitions. Each configuration kk in this grid induces an unknown latency distribution PkP_{k} corresponding to the response times of requests matching the associated method–path pair.

Within each experimental repetition, the data corresponding to the fixed hyperparameter grid are randomly split into a calibration set and a holdout set. Specifically, 30%30\% of the data are allocated to calibration and the remaining 70%70\% to holdout. Using the calibration data, we compute the empirical mean latency for each configuration and select a subset 𝒦⊆{1,…,K}\mathcal{K}\subseteq\{1,\dots,K\} consisting of the MM configurations with the smallest empirical mean latency. This selection rule is fully data-dependent and reuses the same samples later employed to construct confidence bands.

For each selected configuration k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K}, we construct two-sided uniform CDF confidence bands using the methodology described in Section 3. To study the effect of the e-calibrator on both inferential tightness and post-selection reliability, we compare three members of the power-family of e-calibrators (12), and consider three parameters τ∈{1/3, 1/2, 2/3}\tau\in\{1/3,\;1/2,\;2/3\}. For each calibrator, the corresponding band width is computed according to (14), and the same selected set 𝒦\mathcal{K} is used across all calibrators within each repetition to enable a fair comparison.

G.2.2 Results

Because the true latency distributions are unknown, we assess post-selection validity using the empirical CDF computed on the holdout set as a proxy for the true CDF. A band is declared to fail if the holdout empirical CDF exits the proposed interval at any point. We repeat the entire procedure over 300 independent random splits and compute the FCP for each repetition.

Fig. 11 compares post-selection CDF bands constructed using three different e-calibrators for a representative selected configuration. All curves share the same empirical CDF, while the shaded regions correspond to the confidence bands induced by the different values of τ\tau. The resulting band widths vary with the choice of calibrator. In our experiment, the tightest band among the tested calibrators is obtained for τ=1/3\tau=1/3, while both larger and smaller values of τ\tau produce slightly wider bands. This behavior reflects the trade-off introduced by the e-calibrator in the inversion of the e-value tests: different calibrators allocate evidence differently across the range of pp-values, which in turn affects the resulting confidence radius in (14). These results illustrate that the choice of calibrator can have a noticeable effect on inferential tightness, and that intermediate values of τ\tau may provide the most informative bands in practice.
